title: Generating the Unheard: Phylogeny-Guided Latent Generation for Ancestral Sound Reconstruction
claim: Only leaf nodes have observed data; internal ancestors are unobserved, and our method generates plausible outputs for them.
layout: 1 panel, top-down phylogenetic tree with spectrogram callouts, legend top-left, caption box bottom
description: A single large phylogenetic tree titled 'What did ancestral species sound like?' with small bird icons flanking the title. A legend at top-left distinguishes observed extant species (solid dark green dots), unobserved ancestors (dotted circles with question marks) and reconstructed ancestors (orange-ringed circles). Dark green branches descend from a root node to six leaf nodes. Each leaf links to a boxed orange-yellow mel spectrogram labelled Extant species 1–6. Reconstructed internal nodes (root, A, B) have red-outlined callout boxes with generated spectrograms. Arrows at top contrast 'Extant species observed' with 'Generated ancestral vocalizations'. A bottom banner states that real audio exists only at the leaves while the method reconstructs ancestral vocalizations. The eye goes first to the title, then the tree.
caption: Motivation. Extant species at tree leaves have observed vocalizations (mel spectrograms); internal nodes correspond to unobserved ancestors. Our method reconstructs ancestral vocalizations by performing evolutionary inference in a learned latent trait space and decoding back to audio, producing novel spectrograms consistent with descendant species.
abstract: What did an ancestral bird species sound like? Existing ancestral state reconstruction methods can infer low-dimensional traits such as morphological characters at internal nodes of a phylogenetic tree, but no one has tried to produce rich perceptual signals such as audio. Some of the challenges include inferred representations that are either too low-dimensional to decode or lie in non-generative feature spaces, so no method to date can produce ancestral audio. We introduce the first framework that generates plausible ancestral vocalizations. Our pipeline encodes bird recordings into a VAE latent space, learns a low-dimensional trait projection aligned with phylogenetic distances, performs ancestral inference in this trait space, and recovers decodable latents through an anchored inverse lift before emitting novel waveforms for each ancestral node. Because the entire pipeline stays within a decodable latent space, every internal node receives a genuinely new audio output representing plausible intermediate ancestral sounds unavailable to retrieval-based alternatives. Experiments on two phylogenetically distant bird clades, 21-species Tyrannidae and 19-species Paridae, show that our method is the only approach that simultaneously achieves genuine generation, phylogenetic consistency, and naturalistic audio quality across both datasets.
